title: How A Simple Preview Can Improve Behavior And Motivation or-and-motivation/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin highlights a frequently overlooked opportunity during transitions: previewing the upcoming lesson or activity before giving the signal to move on. He recommends including three specific details in the preview — how long the activity will take, what the teacher will be doing, and what students themselves will be doing — arguing that this brief, two-minute investment removes anxiety over the unknown and gives students a mental outline to visualize themselves succeeding within. He notes that selling the content of the lesson as part of the preview can also be highly motivational, helping students look forward to even difficult stretches of the day. By contrast, diving straight into instruction without a preview leaves students antsy, clock-watching, and prone to misbehavior. He clarifies that the preview is separate from the actual lesson content that follows the transition, functioning purely as preparatory framing.
points: Previewing an upcoming lesson before transitioning removes anxiety over the unknown and gives students a mental outline to follow.
An effective preview includes three details: how long it will take, what the teacher will do, and what students themselves will do.
Using the preview to "sell" the upcoming content can be highly motivational, even for difficult stretches of the day.
Skipping the preview and diving straight into instruction tends to leave students antsy, clock-watching, and prone to misbehavior.
The preview is distinct from the lesson itself — it functions purely as brief preparatory framing before the transition.
quotes: But in doing so, you pass up an opportunity to ensure that that next thing goes according to plan.
The way it works is that just before giving your signal to transition, you’re going to preview the next lesson or activity.
I’m going to be telling you an amazing story about a thirteen-year-old boy that you’re not going to believe.
Because when your students know what to expect, they’re able to relax, live in the moment, and focus on whatever you lay out before them.
And when you use the preview to sell what it is you have to teach them (#2), it can also be highly motivational.
When students don't know what to expect, on the other hand, when you dive straightaway into your lessons, they become antsy and excitable.
It comforts. It focuses. It builds anticipation. It opens the door to a class that is ready to learn.
